issues.legal_issue: A decree entered against an original defendant after the defendant’s interest has devolved is not executable against the successor who was not made a party to the suit.
material_facts: The State acquired the relevant division while the suit was pending.
The suit was decreed against the original defendant after that acquisition, without the State being added as a party.
The decree-holder later sought to execute the decree against the State.
The plaintiff had not sought leave to continue the suit against the State.
issues.conclusion: Shah J. held that the decree was not binding on, and could not be executed against, the State, and allowed the appeal. The concluding order in the supplied text records a difference of opinion and directs that the matter be placed before a larger Bench.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 10 CPC permits a suit to be continued against a person upon whom an interest devolves during the suit, with leave of the court; the plaintiff who seeks to continue against that person normally must apply for leave. Section 47 CPC places execution questions before the executing court. Sections 50 and 52 concern execution against legal representatives in specified circumstances and do not authorize execution against a successor who was not brought on record after devolution during the suit. The Court distinguished State of Orissa v. Klockner and Company, which addressed successor-in-interest status but not this execution issue, and Bhagwan Dass Chopra v. United Bank of India, which concerned proceedings under the Industrial Disputes Act. It relied on Dhurandhar Prasad Singh v. Jai Prakash University for the requirement of leave under Order XXII Rule 10, and distinguished Rai Charan Mandal v. Biswanath Mandal and Mahanth Harihar Gir v. Karu Lal on their facts.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and interest_devolved_during_pending_suit and decree_entered_after_devolution and successor_not_made_party and plaintiff_did_not_seek_leave

predicates.execution_proceeding: A decree-holder sought to enforce a decree against a successor to an original defendant.
predicates.interest_devolved_during_pending_suit: The original defendant’s interest passed to a successor while the suit was pending.
predicates.decree_entered_after_devolution: The court entered the decree after the interest had passed to the successor.
predicates.successor_not_made_party: The successor was not added as a party to the suit before the decree was entered.
predicates.plaintiff_did_not_seek_leave: The plaintiff did not seek the court’s permission to continue the suit against the successor.
predicates.decree_not_executable_against_successor: The decree cannot be enforced against the successor.

issues.definition: When execution is sought against a successor whose interest arose during the pending suit, and the decree was entered without the successor being made a party after the plaintiff failed to seek leave to continue against the successor, the decree cannot be enforced against that successor.

issues.legal_issue: When a defendant’s interest devolves during a pending suit, continuing the suit against the successor requires leave of the court, which the plaintiff seeking that continuation normally must obtain.
material_facts: The relevant interest passed to the State while the suit was pending.
The plaintiff continued the suit against the original defendant without applying to add the State as successor or obtaining leave to proceed against it.
issues.conclusion: Shah J. held that Order XXII Rule 10 is an enabling provision, that leave is required to continue a suit against a person upon whom the defendant’s interest has devolved, and that the plaintiff normally bears the initial duty to apply when the devolution is known or could have been discovered with due diligence.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 10 CPC provides that, where an interest is assigned, created or devolves during a suit, the suit may by leave of the court be continued by or against the person to or upon whom the interest has passed. It does not provide that the suit abates. Dhurandhar Prasad Singh v. Jai Prakash University states that leave must be obtained for continuation against a person upon whom the defendant’s interest has devolved and that, as a rule of prudence, the plaintiff initially must apply when the devolution is known or could have been discovered with due diligence.

predicates.pending_suit: A suit remained pending when the relevant interest passed from a defendant.
predicates.defendant_interest_devolved: A defendant’s interest passed to another person during the suit.
predicates.plaintiff_seeks_to_continue_against_succ: The plaintiff sought to pursue the pending suit against the person who received the defendant’s interest.
predicates.plaintiff_must_obtain_leave_to_continue_: The plaintiff must obtain the court’s leave to continue the suit against that successor.

issues.definition: If a defendant’s interest passes to another person during a pending suit and the plaintiff seeks to proceed against that person, the plaintiff must obtain leave to continue against the successor.
